title: Given a dictionary of root words and a sentence, replace every word in the sentence that has a root in the dictionary as a prefix with the shortest such root. Return the resulting sentence.
shortTitle: Replace Words — Trie for shortest prefix (root) replacement

s1_definition.profdef: Replace Words inserts every root into a Trie, then for each word in the sentence walks the Trie character by character and replaces the word with the first root encountered, which is the shortest matching prefix. If no root prefixes the word, the word is left unchanged.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the bank normalizing long product names to their shortest official code. You keep a directory of official short codes, and whenever a customer types a long product name, you walk the name letter by letter against the directory and the moment you complete an official code you stop and swap the long name for that short code. If you never complete any official code, you keep the name as-is.
s1_definition.oneliner: Insert roots into a Trie, then for each sentence word walk the Trie and replace it with the first (shortest) root hit, else leave it unchanged.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Replace Words inserts every root into a Trie, then for each word in the sentence walks the Trie character by character and replaces the word with the first root encountered, which is the shortest matching prefix. If no root prefixes the word, the word is left unchanged.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the bank normalizing long product names to their shortest official code. You keep a directory of official short codes, and whenever a customer types a long product name, you walk the name letter by letter against the directory and the moment you complete an official code you stop and swap the long name for that short code. If you never complete any official code, you keep the name as-is.

**One line to remember:** Insert roots into a Trie, then for each sentence word walk the Trie and replace it with the first (shortest) root hit, else leave it unchanged.

sections.s2_technical:
Insert every root into a Trie with an end-of-word flag so that reaching a flagged node means a complete root has been matched. For example: mark `node.isWord = true;` at the end of each root insert.

For each word in the sentence, walk the Trie from the root following the word's characters. The moment the walk reaches a node whose end-of-word flag is set, stop and use the prefix walked so far as the replacement, because the first flagged node encountered is necessarily the shortest root that prefixes the word. For example: `if (node.isWord) return prefixSoFar;`.

If the walk falls off the Trie, meaning a character has no child, or reaches the end of the word without ever hitting a flagged node, the original word is kept unchanged. The replacement is applied per word and the words are rejoined with spaces.

The time cost is the total number of characters across all sentence words, since each character is examined at most once during its word's walk, plus the cost of building the Trie from the roots. A senior nuance is that stopping at the first flagged node guarantees the shortest root without sorting roots by length, and that a word is only replaced when a full root is matched, not merely when characters happen to line up.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, free-text product descriptions must be normalized to the shortest official product root code before analytics. The system must replace each descriptive word with its shortest matching official root, or leave it alone if none matches. This is exactly how Replace Words works — the first root hit while walking the Trie is the shortest prefix.

Problem 2 — The dictionary of official roots is large, and normalization must be fast over long descriptions. This is exactly why a Trie walk per word, stopping at the first root, is used.

The mini-project builds a `ProductRootNormalizer` service, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo that normalizes a product description sentence.

sections.s5_journey:
The input roots are sav, loan, card, and the sentence is "savings loanaccount cardholder current".

Step 1: The constructor inserts sav, loan, and card into the Trie, flagging the terminal node of each.

Step 2: The word savings walks s, a, v, and at v the end-of-word flag is set, so the walk stops and the word is replaced with sav.

Step 3: The word loanaccount walks l, o, a, n, and at n the flag is set, so it is replaced with loan, the remaining account characters never being examined.

Step 4: The word cardholder walks c, a, r, d, hits the flag at d, and is replaced with card.

Step 5: The word current walks c, u, but the Trie c node has no u child, so the walk falls off and current is kept unchanged.

Step 6: The words are rejoined with spaces to produce "sav loan card current".

```text
2026-10-26T20:40:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Product Description Normalizer
2026-10-26T20:40:00Z [INFO] Normalized: 'savings loanaccount cardholder current' -> 'sav loan card current'
```

```text
                   └─c─a─r─d●

  savings      → s,a,v hits ● → "sav"   (stop at first root)
  loanaccount  → l,o,a,n hits ● → "loan" (rest ignored)
  cardholder   → c,a,r,d hits ● → "card"
  current      → c,u : no 'u' child → unchanged "current"
  Result: "sav loan card current"
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Replace Words asks me to swap each word of a sentence for the shortest dictionary root that prefixes it, leaving words with no matching root untouched. My solution inserts every root into a Trie with an end-of-word flag, then processes each sentence word by walking the Trie character by character.

The key insight is that the first flagged node I encounter while walking is automatically the shortest root, because flagged nodes appear in increasing prefix length along a path. So the moment the walk reaches an end-of-word node, I stop and return the prefix walked so far as the replacement, without needing to sort roots by length or examine the rest of the word. If the walk falls off the Trie because a character has no child, or if it reaches the end of the word without hitting any flagged node, I keep the original word.

What interviewers check is that I stop at the first root rather than the longest, that I only replace on a genuine end-of-word match rather than on partial character alignment, and that the overall cost is linear in the total characters of the sentence plus the Trie build. This is cleaner and faster than comparing each word against every root.

In my project at National Bank of India, I used this to normalize free-text product descriptions to their shortest official root code before feeding analytics. Each descriptive word was walked against a Trie of official roots and collapsed to the first root it completed, so savings became sav and loanaccount became loan, while words with no official root, like current, passed through unchanged. Stopping at the first root kept normalization fast even over long descriptions and a large root dictionary.
